doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Comedy timing and entertaining an audience
summary: What jazz players learned from comedy about pacing and audience.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: [partially inaudible question about relationship between comedy, comedy teams, timing, and how to grasp an audience]

It had to do with your delivery, when and where to do your most important things in your act, when to hold back, and how to disperse them evenly so that you wouldn’t do everything you did right now and be standing out there looking stupid. It taught you a way of spreading out your talents, which of course brought more appreciation for the people you were performing for and to you, because you could sustain it. A lot of things we learned from comedy: timing, as far as when not to do things - it’s not a good time – when not to play certain tunes for certain audiences. Then there’s certain audiences that are geared for lighter things. They want some fun. So you play these things, and you’re in. But if you – for instance, take Mumbles, the tune that I’ve been associated with. I know when to and when not to do Mumbles. If I do that in one of those hoity-toity atmospheres, somebody might say, “What in the world is he doing, George? What is he saying?” But in the right crowd, it’s just fun.
